before.claim: After nuclear segregation in eukaryotes, cytokinesis partitions the parental cytoplasm. In animal cells, a contractile ring containing actin and myosin constricts the membrane at a cleavage furrow. In plant cells, membrane-bound vesicles fuse at the equator to form a cell plate that develops into new membranes and wall material.

A rigid plant wall generally prevents a deep cleavage furrow like that of an animal cell. Both mechanisms divide the contents of one cell, but their membrane trafficking and force-generation mechanisms differ substantially.

Animal cytokinesis uses an actin–myosin contractile ring that constricts the plasma membrane. In walled plant cells, membrane-bound vesicles contribute to a cell plate that develops into new separating membranes and cell-wall material. Cytokinesis partitions cytoplasm; mitosis is the preceding nuclear segregation process.

In an animal cell, a contractile ring forms a cleavage furrow and constricts the plasma membrane until daughter cells separate. In a typical plant cell, rigid walls prevent an equivalent constriction; vesicles assemble a cell plate between the daughter nuclei that develops into new membranes and wall material. These are alternative mechanisms for dividing the cytoplasm after nuclear division, not alternative ways to segregate chromosomes. Both must deliver sufficient cytoplasm and essential organelles to the resulting cells.

after.claim: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm between daughter cells. In animal cells, a contractile ring of actin and myosin constricts the plasma membrane at a cleavage furrow until the daughters separate.

before.claim: Cytokinesis often yields daughter cells of similar size, but unequal partitioning is important in some biological contexts. During human oogenesis, one division yields a large cell and a small polar body; budding yeast forms a smaller bud and a larger parent-like compartment.

Each functional daughter must receive essential machinery, including organelles whose production depends on pre-existing structures, such as mitochondria. Unequal cytoplasm does not mean one daughter necessarily gets no DNA; nuclear segregation must still be considered separately.

Equal cytokinesis usually supplies two similar daughter-cell volumes. Unequal examples include budding yeast and human oogenesis, in which one cell retains most of the cytoplasm while polar bodies receive far less. Both daughters must still inherit adequate essential cellular structures; mitochondria arise by division of existing organelles.

Equal cytokinesis creates daughter cells of approximately similar cytoplasmic volume, but some developmental divisions deliberately generate unequal daughters. In oogenesis, unequal cytokinesis preserves most cytoplasm in the future ovum while small polar bodies receive far less. A developing embryo may also use asymmetric division to establish different cell fates. The nuclei may still contain the appropriate chromosome complement even when the cells differ greatly in size. Each viable daughter must receive organelles needed for continued cellular function.

after.claim: Cytokinesis usually divides cytoplasm approximately equally, but not always. Human oogenesis retains most cytoplasm in the large future ovum while producing small polar bodies. In budding yeast, a smaller bud separates from the larger parent cell.

In the eukaryotic cells considered here, each daughter must receive at least one mitochondrion and any other essential organelle made only by growth and division of a pre-existing structure. Unequal cell size does not itself mean unequal chromosome number; nuclear segregation and cytoplasmic allocation are distinct.

before.claim: Mitosis is nuclear division that normally preserves chromosome number, producing genetically similar nuclei when segregation is accurate. Meiosis is a specialized nuclear division that halves chromosome number and makes genetically varied haploid nuclei for a sexual life cycle.

When a eukaryotic cell divides, chromosomes must be separated to prevent most daughters from being left without a nucleus. Mitosis involves one round of nuclear division following replication; meiosis includes two divisions after one round of DNA replication.

Mitosis preserves chromosome number and ordinarily produces genetically similar nuclei for growth and repair. Meiosis requires two nuclear divisions after one round of DNA replication and creates haploid nuclei for sexual reproduction. Nuclear division before cell separation helps avoid daughters lacking a nucleus in typical nucleated eukaryotic cells.

Mitosis generally yields nuclei with the same chromosome complement as the parent nucleus and supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis instead consists of two nuclear divisions after one replication, reducing diploid to haploid chromosome number in the products of typical animal gametogenesis. The separation of homologous chromosomes in the first meiotic division is the crucial reduction step. These nuclear processes are not interchangeable with cytokinesis, which physically partitions the cytoplasm after chromosome segregation.

after.claim: Mitosis separates copied chromosomes into nuclei with the same chromosome number and genome, assuming accurate copying and segregation. before.claim: Before either mitosis or meiosis, DNA is replicated in S phase. Each replicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids containing separate DNA double helices joined at the centromere region. Counting chromosomes by centromeres means a chromosome remains one chromosome before its sisters separate.

In a model G1 cell with 2n = 4, there are four unreplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules. After S phase, there are still four chromosomes but eight chromatids and eight DNA molecules. Chromosome number only changes when sisters become independent chromosomes at separation.

Count chromosomes by centromeres rather than visible chromatids: a 2n=4 G1 nucleus has four chromosomes and four DNA molecules; after S phase it still has four chromosomes but eight DNA molecules. During mitotic anaphase separated chromatids become independent chromosomes, temporarily eight in one undivided cell.

In a theoretical diploid cell with 2n = 4, G1 contains four unreplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules. After S phase there are still four chromosomes, but eight sister chromatids and eight DNA molecules. Counting both chromatids as separate chromosomes before their separation gives a misleading chromosome number.

after.claim: DNA replication precedes both mitosis and meiosis. Each replicated chromosome contains two sister chromatids, each with one elongated DNA double helix. Sisters remain attached until their separation at anaphase; in meiosis they normally remain joined through meiosis I and separate in meiosis II.

A model cell with four chromosomes has four DNA molecules before replication. Afterwards it still has four chromosomes, each with two chromatids, so there are eight DNA molecules. Once sister chromatids separate, each counts as an independent chromosome. The cell-cycle phase names are developed in D2.1.13 (HL).

before.claim: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to segregate normally during meiosis. A gamete may receive an extra chromosome or lack one; fertilization can then produce aneuploidy such as trisomy.

Most cases of Down syndrome involve an extra copy of chromosome 21, commonly arising through meiotic nondisjunction. Not every case has the same genetic mechanism and aneuploidies have different developmental outcomes. The extra genetic material affects gene dosage rather than simply substituting one DNA base.

Nondisjunction is failure of appropriate chromosome separation in meiosis I or II, producing gametes with abnormal chromosome counts. Fertilization involving a gamete with an extra chromosome 21 can produce trisomy 21, associated with Down syndrome. Not every case has an identical clinical presentation, and chromosomal dosage—not a single point mutation—is central.

During meiosis I, failure of a pair of homologous chromosomes to separate can leave a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21. A segregation error in meiosis II may similarly produce a gamete with an extra chromosome 21 copy after failure of sister chromatids to separate. Fusion with a normal gamete can then produce a zygote with three copies of chromosome 21, called trisomy 21, which causes most Down syndrome cases. This mechanism concerns chromosome number, not necessarily a mutation in a single gene.

before.claim: The proliferating eukaryotic cell cycle comprises G1, S and G2 within interphase, then mitosis followed by cytokinesis. G1 includes biosynthesis and growth, S includes DNA replication, and G2 prepares for mitotic events and checks whether copying has finished.

Interphase often occupies much more of the cycle than mitosis. DNA synthesis occurs in S, not metaphase. Some cells withdraw from the proliferative cycle into a G0-like quiescent state, so a diagram of continuous cycling is a model rather than a rule for every cell.

The order G1 → S → G2 → mitosis → cytokinesis prevents a cell from allocating unreplicated chromosomes to new daughter cells. Interphase comprises G1, DNA synthesis in S and G2 preparation. The cell cycle is regulated; some specialized cells may pause or leave the active cycle rather than dividing perpetually.

G1 is a period of growth and biosynthesis; S phase duplicates nuclear DNA, and G2 prepares a cell for mitosis. During M phase the replicated chromosomes segregate and cytokinesis commonly produces two daughters. After S phase there are two DNA molecules per replicated chromosome, but the chromosome count remains unchanged until sister chromatids separate. A mitotic index counts the proportion of sampled cells visibly in mitosis, not the number of completed cell divisions per unit time without additional assumptions. The cycle is regulated and not continuously active in every differentiated cell.

before.claim: Proto-oncogenes normally contribute to regulated signals that support growth and division. Certain activating mutations can produce oncogenes with excessive growth-promoting effects. Inactivating mutations in tumor-suppressor genes can remove restraints on proliferation or on damage-response pathways.

The presence of one mutation does not mean cancer is inevitable: multiple controls act and many altered cells do not form tumours.
